concept.name: Implied volatility
concept.definition: The forward-looking volatility value that, when input to an option pricing model such as Black-Scholes, equates the model price to the observed market price of the option. It is the market's consensus expectation of future volatility embedded in option premiums.
concept.intuition: Options cost more when traders expect big moves, so the premium can be read backward: the volatility that justifies today's option price is what the market collectively expects.
concept.mechanics: Holding spot, strike, rate, and time to expiry fixed, invert the pricing model numerically (bisection or Newton-Raphson) on the observed option price; no closed-form inverse exists for Black-Scholes. Index-level composites such as VIX aggregate implied volatilities across strikes.
concept.formula: IV = sigma such that C_BS(S, K, r, T, sigma) = C_market, where C_BS is the Black-Scholes call price with spot S, strike K, rate r, and time to expiry T.
concept.failure_modes: IV is model-dependent and inherits the pricing model's assumptions; it can embed skew, event premium, and supply-demand distortions rather than pure volatility expectations. Being an expectation, it can diverge widely from the volatility that actually realizes.
concept.misconceptions: IV is not a directional forecast: it says how much movement is expected, not which way. High IV does not mean price will fall, and low IV does not mean it must rise.
concept.example: If an at-the-money one-month option's premium solves Black-Scholes only at sigma = 25%, the implied volatility is 25% annualized; if the underlying then realizes 12% over the year, IV overshot.
